procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 27.11.2019 of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in CRLA No.1217 of 2015
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Kerala issued a Judgment and Order on 27.11.2019 in CRLA No.1217 of 2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's Judgment and Order. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding it lacking in merit.

directions: The appellant who is in jail may, in usual course, be at liberty to apply for remission in accordance with the prevailing policy of the State.

issue.issue_text: Whether in the circumstances of the instant case, the appellant had any premeditated mind to kill the deceased or was it due to grave and sudden provocation which would not amount to murder or would at best be a case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend up to 10 years or with ﬁ ne or with both u/s. 304 Part-II of IPC.

facts.fact: There was a history of the appellant harassing his deceased wife, including demands for dowry and frequent assaults while he was intoxicated.
On the day of the incident, the quarrel was not a single, sudden event. A neighbor (PW1) had visited earlier, saw injuries on the wife from the assault, and left because of the ongoing fight.
After the neighbor left, the deceased wife poured kerosene on herself. The appellant, seeing her in this state, took a matchstick, lit it, and threw it on her body, saying, "You Die".

law.law_name: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)
law.description: This exception reduces a charge of murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the act is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and provided the offender has not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.

application.reasoning: The Court determined the fight was not 'sudden' as required by the exception. It was part of an ongoing history of quarrels and had been happening for some time on the day of the incident, as evidenced by the neighbor's testimony. There was a sufficient time gap between the initial assault and the final act of setting her on fire.

The Court found that the appellant's actions demonstrated a 'premeditated mind'. Seeing his wife drenched in kerosene and then consciously lighting a match to set her ablaze was not an impulsive act but a deliberate one, showing an intention to kill.

Most importantly, the Court held that the appellant took 'undue advantage' of the situation. When the deceased was in a vulnerable state covered in kerosene, the appellant exploited this to light her on fire. This act of taking undue advantage explicitly disqualifies him from the benefit of Exception 4.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that his actions constituted murder under Section 302 IPC, not culpable homicide under Section 304 Part-II. The Court found that the conditions for Exception 4 to Section 300 were not met because the quarrel was not sudden, the act was premeditated, and the appellant took undue advantage of the situation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether in the circumstances of the instant case, the appellant had any premeditated mind to kill the deceased or was it due to grave and sudden provocation which would not amount to murder or would at best be a case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend up to 10 years or with ﬁ ne or with both u/s. 304 Part-II of IPC.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that he had no premeditated mind or intention to kill his deceased wife.
Consequently, the provisions of Section 302 IPC (murder) are not applicable, and at best, he should be charged under Section 304 Part-II of the IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder).
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the appellant burnt his deceased wife with a matchstick, fully knowing that she was drenched in kerosene oil.
The act of lighting a matchstick and throwing it upon her would certainly cause her death, indicating intent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is immaterial in such cases which party oﬀ ers the provocation or commits the ﬁ rst assault.
obiter: The appellant who is in jail may, in usual course, be at liberty to apply for remission in accordance with the prevailing policy of the State.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC because he took "undue advantage" of the situation. Upon seeing his wife drenched in kerosene, the appellant consciously took advantage of her vulnerable state by lighting a matchstick and throwing it upon her, an act he knew would result in her death. This action negates the possibility of classifying the offense as culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
legal_tests_applied: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, which requires that for culpable homicide not to be murder, it must be committed without a premeditated mind, in a sudden fight or quarrel, and crucially, without the offender taking "undue advantage" of the situation.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant, upon seeing the deceased drenched in kerosene, clearly took advantage of the situation and lighted a matchstick and threw it upon her so that she can be burnt.
The appellant having taken “undue advantage” of the situation cannot be extended the beneﬁt of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC so as to bring the case within the ambit of Part-II of 304 IPC.
There was suﬃcient time in between the two acts [the quarrel and the burning] and it cannot be said that there was a sudden quarrel and provocation leading to burning.
The appellant saw the deceased wife drenched in kerosene and was conscious that if lighted, she would be burnt to death even then ignited her to ﬁre. This shows premeditated mind to kill her.
why_respondent_won: The appellant had burnt the deceased wife with a matchstick fully knowing that she was drenched in kerosene oil and that lightning of matchstick and throwing it upon her would certainly cause her death.
The evidence clinches the issue and establishes beyond doubt that the appellant is guilty of the oﬀence of culpable homicide amounting to murder.
